background_notes.fact: For a continuous Banach-space-valued function G on a compact interval [c,d], ||integral_c^d G(t)dt||<=integral_c^d||G(t)||dt<=(d-c)sup||G||. For a C^1 Banach-space-valued function F, F(t)-F(c)=integral_c^t F'(s)ds. Suprema and essential suprema do not increase on restriction to a subinterval; in particular the X norm in D020 does not increase on restriction. These apply to each smooth step here, including partial steps.

background_notes.justification: The integral norm inequality follows by the triangle inequality for Riemann sums and passage to the defining norm limit of the integral. The fundamental theorem follows by integrating the continuous derivative, or by applying continuous linear functionals and the scalar theorem. Restricting a bounded function reduces the set over which its supremum is taken, and the distributional derivative restricts to the derivative on the smaller interval.

background_notes.fact: For a smooth solution u of D012 and v(t)=S_{-t}u(t), v'(t)=(1/2)Bop_t(v(t),v(t)). It is real and mean-zero. A continuous function which is C^1 on each of finitely many adjoining time intervals has distributional derivative equal to its piecewise derivative, without point masses at the joins; this applies to e=v-V.

background_notes.justification: Differentiate v=S_{-t}u: v'=S_{-t}(u_t+partial_x^3 u)=(1/2)S_{-t}partial_x(u^2); the Fourier multipliers give S_t v=u. Smooth periodic functions have rapidly decreasing Fourier coefficients, locally uniformly with their time derivatives, so these differentiations and spatial operations are legitimate. Reality and zero mean follow from D012 and N005. Integrating against a smooth compactly supported time test function on each piece cancels the boundary terms at each join by continuity, proving the distributional assertion.
